II. 
Purpose of Testimony and Overview of Filing 
10 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the Panel’s testimony? 
11 
A. 
The purpose of the Panel’s testimony is to support the Company’s request to 
12 
increase its electric and gas delivery rates.  In support of this request, the Panel 
13 
will: 
14 
(i) 
present Niagara Mohawk’s historic and forecast data for various periods 
15 
in a manner consistent with the Commission’s regulations and policies; 
16 
(ii) 
summarize the steps taken to mitigate the rate request in recognition of 
17 
the public health emergency and economic downturn caused by the 
18 
ongoing COVID-19 pandemic;  
19 


--- Page 11 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 8 of 146 
(iii) 
describe the Company’s forecast of operation and maintenance 
1 
(“O&M”) expenses, as well as adjustments to those expenses that were 
2 
made to normalize the historic test year amounts; 
3 
(iv) 
describe the Company’s efforts to reduce its cost of service and detail 
4 
how savings related to specific Company productivity initiatives were 
5 
reflected in the filings; 
6 
(v) 
discuss the development of Niagara Mohawk’s electric and gas rate 
7 
bases; 
8 
(vi) 
support the Company’s forecast and amortization of regulatory deferral 
9 
balances; and  
10 
(vii) 
describe proposed treatment for deferrals that the Commission has 
11 
previously adopted, as well as proposed new deferral mechanisms.  
12 
 
13 
The Panel will also describe the Company’s efforts in connection with the 
14 
preparation of these rate filings to review the accuracy of costs in the historic 
15 
test year and to appropriately normalize these results for known and measurable 
16 
changes that will occur between the end of the historic test year and the rate 
17 
year. 
18 
 
19

Q. 
What is the historic test year in these proceedings?   
14 
A. 
The historic test year in these proceedings is the twelve months ended 
15 
December 31, 2019 (“Historic Test Year”).  The Historic Test Year data 
16 
consists of the costs recorded on the books of Niagara Mohawk, including:  (i) 
17 
costs incurred directly by the Company; (ii) costs charged to Niagara Mohawk 
18 
from National Grid Service Company and National Grid Engineering & Survey, 
19 
Inc. (collectively, the “Service Company”); and (iii) costs charged to Niagara 
20 
Mohawk from other affiliated companies.   
21 
 
22 
Q. 
What Historic Test Year and rate year information is the Company 
23 
presenting? 
24 
A. 
The Company is presenting electric and gas operating results for the Historic 
25 
Test Year and forecast data for the rate year, which is the twelve months ending 
26 
June 30, 2022 (“Rate Year”).  In addition, the Company is including forecast 
27 


--- Page 14 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 11 of 146 
data for the twelve months ending June 30, 2023 (“Data Year 1”), and June 30, 
1 
2024 (“Data Year 2”) (collectively, the “Data Years”) to facilitate a multi-year 
2 
rate settlement in these proceedings.  The forecast data provides the basis for 
3 
computing the revenue requirement for the Rate Year and Data Years in these 
4 
proceedings.  The information presented in these filings is consistent with that 
5 
required under the Commission’s “Statement of Policy on Test Periods in Major 
6 
Rate Proceedings.” 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
You mentioned that you have provided data to support a multi-year 
9 
settlement.  Do you believe that it is especially important in this case for 
10 
the parties to explore a multi-year settlement? 
11 
A. 
Yes.  As discussed further below, in preparing these filings, in recognition of 
12 
the severe impact that the COVID-19 pandemic is having on the economy of 
13 
New York State, the Company included a number of proposals that are intended 
14 
to mitigate the impact of the filings on customers’ bills during the Rate Year, in 
15 
a number of cases pushing the impact of certain proposals out into the Data 
16 
Years.  Moreover, the Company is committed to working with all interested 
17 
stakeholders to find ways to further reduce the Rate Year impact through the 
18 
settlement process.  The Company strongly believes that a multi-year resolution 
19 
of these proceedings is in the best interest of all parties. 
20 
 
21 


--- Page 15 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 12 of 146 
Q. 
How has the Company presented its projected capital and O&M 
1 
expenditures in this case? 
2 
A.        The Company had planned to file this case by the end of April 2020 to enable 
3 
new rates to become effective April 1, 2021, with the planned Rate Year being 
4 
April 1, 2021 – March 31, 2022.  This would have coincided with the end of 
5 
the current three-year rate plan under which the Company is operating that was 
6 
approved in the 2017 Rate Case.  Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the 
7 
Company deferred filing this rate case by three months.  As a result, under the 
8 
procedural schedule applicable to most major utility rate cases, new rates to 
9 
replace expiring rates from the Company’s most recent rate plan would not go 
10 
into effect until July 1, 2021, and the corresponding rate year would be from 
11 
July 1, 2021 – June 30, 2022.   
12 
 
13 
 
The Company operates on a fiscal year (“FY”) that runs from April 1 through 
14 
March 31.  Thus, FY 2022 is the twelve-month period April 1, 2021 – March 
15 
31, 2022.  National Grid typically creates its capital plans and operating expense 
16 
budgets on a fiscal year basis.  To present the Rate Year and Data Year revenue 
17 
requirements reflected in this case, the Company used the FY capital plan 
18 
forecasts of the different operating groups in this case (i.e., the electric business, 
19 
the gas business, IT, Shared Services, etc.) and determined the monthly cash 
20 


--- Page 16 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 13 of 146 
flow associated with that capital investment to develop rate year schedules 
1 
presented in the exhibits of this panel.  
2 
 
3 
 
Regarding projected operating expenses, the core of the Company’s revenue 
4 
requirement is based on normalized Historic Test Year costs adjusted by 
5 
inflation to the Rate Year.  The Company adjusts this normalized and inflated 
6 
Historic Test Year amount for any incremental amounts associated with known 
7 
and measurable changes projected for the Rate Year or Data Years.  Such 
8 
incremental amounts are reflected in the Company’s Operating Expense Exhibit 
9 
___ (RRP-3). 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
What are Niagara Mohawk’s Rate Year revenue requirements and 
12 
associated revenue deficiencies based on current rates for the electric and 
13 
gas businesses? 
14 
A. 
Based on the cost of services set forth in the Company’s filings, for the Rate 
15 
Year, Niagara Mohawk’s revenue deficiency is $100.407 million for the electric 
16 
business and $41.818 million for the gas business, based on a 9.50 percent 
17 
return on equity (“ROE”) and a 48.00 percent common equity ratio, as 
18 
recommended by the Company’s Return on Equity Panel.  If a multi-year 
19 
settlement is reached, the Company proposes that a ROE of 10.00 percent be 
20 


--- Page 17 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 14 of 146 
used to calculate the revenue requirement, as recommended by the Return on 
1 
Equity Panel.   
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Did the Company take specific action to modify its requested rate relief in 
4 
the Rate Year in light of the COVID-19 pandemic? 
5 
A. 
Yes.  The Company made every effort to moderate the proposals in these filings 
6 
and the resulting bill impacts.  To that end, the Company is interested in 
7 
exploring a multi-year rate plan that would allow the Company to take full 
8 
advantage of efficiencies (described below) and manage bills over a three-year 
9 
period – with the goal of minimizing any increase in the first year of the rate 
10 
plan when the ongoing economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic are 
11 
anticipated to be the most severe.  Among other opportunities, the Company is 
12 
well-positioned to leverage regulatory deferrals, as discussed later in this 
13 
testimony.    
14 
 
15 
In specific consideration of the pandemic, the Company took several actions to 
16 
moderate its costs of providing service, including:   
17 
• Gas Depreciation Expense.  Modified its gas depreciation proposals to 
18 
delay the proposed commencement of a more rapid amortization of leak 
19 
prone pipe that is being replaced from the Rate Year to Data Year 1, and 
20 
the commencement of the proposed recovery of a depreciation reserve 
21 


--- Page 18 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 15 of 146 
deficiency from the Rate Year to Date Year 2.  These modifications 
1 
reduced Rate Year depreciation expense by approximately $18 million. 
2 
• Issued New Long-term Debt.  Issued $1.1 billion of new long-term debt, 
3 
including $600 million of so-called “green bonds” that took advantage 
4 
of certain historic lows in bond yields for companies with strong credit 
5 
ratings, reducing the projected cost of debt by an estimated 41 basis 
6 
points and resulting in approximately $16 million of annual interest 
7 
savings. 
8 
• Management Wages.  Reduced its scheduled July 1, 2020 management 
9 
wage increase from 3.25 percent to 1.91 percent, resulting in savings of 
10 
$1.6 million. 
11 
• Capital Spending Reductions.  Carefully reviewed and modified the 
12 
capital spending program for both its gas and electric businesses.  The 
13 
result of these efforts was that near-term spending in the Rate Year was 
14 
reduced by tens of millions of dollars. 
15 
• Excess Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes.  Accelerated the return to 
16 
customers of unprotected excess deferred income taxes resulting from 
17 
the passage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.  This reduced the 
18 
Rate Year revenue requirement by approximately $60 million (total 
19 
electric and gas). 
20 


--- Page 19 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 16 of 146 
• Electric and Gas Sales Forecasts.  Reflected the anticipated economic 
1 
impacts of the pandemic on customer demand in the electric and gas 
2 
sales forecasts. 
3 
• Efficiency Efforts.  Reflected efficiency savings over the three-year term 
4 
of the proposed rate plan of more than $140 million through proactive 
5 
efforts undertaken by National Grid to reduce costs for customers.  
6 
These savings far exceed those typically included in a one-year rate 
7 
filing and serve to benefit customers during this challenging time. 
8 
 
9 
In addition, it should be recognized that a significant portion of the Company’s 
10 
request for rate relief arises from the fact that its electric revenues have declined 
11 
significantly as a result of reduced electric usage by commercial and industrial 
12 
customers during the pandemic.  If the Company had not made these filings, it 
13 
would have recovered these lost revenues through the normal operation of its 
14 
revenue decoupling mechanism (“RDM”).  The Company estimates that 
15 
approximately $40 million of its proposed electric commercial and industrial 
16

Trend Analysis 
9 
Q. 
Did the Company compare Historic Test Year O&M costs with prior 
10 
period costs?   
11 
A. 
Yes.  The Company performed an analysis to look at changes in expenses 
12 
incurred by the Company from calendar year (“CY”) 2016 through the Historic 
13 
Test Year.  The purpose of the review was to look at trends in costs by 
14 
functional area incurred by the Company directly, as well as from the Service 
15 
Company and affiliates that charge the Company.  The Company’s costs must 
16 
be examined on a total basis to draw meaningful conclusions regarding year-
17 
over-year variations.  This examination was accomplished by combining (i) 
18 
costs incurred directly by the Company, (ii) costs charged to the Company from 
19 
the Service Company, and (iii) costs charged to the Company from other 
20 
affiliates.   
21 


--- Page 36 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 33 of 146 
The analysis of costs based on the combination of direct and indirect charges 
1 
provides improved clarity concerning the factors driving cost increases and 
2 
decreases by removing the impact of organizational changes that merely result 
3 
in shifts rather than absolute changes in costs from year to year.  Exhibit __ 
4 
(RRP-2), Schedule 4 presents a comparison of total O&M costs for the period 
5 
from CY 2016 through the Historic Test Year. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
What does Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 show? 
8 
A. 
The analysis presented on Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 shows that for the 
9 
period 2016 through December 31, 2019, the total electric O&M costs incurred 
10 
by Niagara Mohawk increased from $1.5 billion to $1.7 billion, an increase of 
11 
$195 million.  The $195 million difference reflects significant increases in the 
12 
Company’s energy efficiency programs (“DSM”) costs excluded from base 
13 
rates of $146 million, Energy Transition Implementation Plans of $52 million, 
14 
included within “Customer Operations”), and storm costs of $75 million).  
15 
Offsetting those increases were decreased purchase power costs of $43 million, 
16 
pension and other post-employment benefits costs of $17 million, and 
17 
regulatory assessment costs of $17 million. 
18 
Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 also shows that, over the period 2016 through 
19 
December 31, 2019, the total gas O&M costs incurred by Niagara Mohawk 
20 
increased from $307 million to $405 million, an increase of $97 million.  The 
21 


--- Page 37 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 34 of 146 
$97 million difference includes significant increases in the Company’s gas 
1 
supply costs of $98 million and increased operational work load within the Gas 
2 
Business Unit of $15 million.  Offsetting those increases were decreases in 
3 
DSM of $10 million, and regulatory assessments of $6 million.   
4 
 
 
5 
 
Regarding the source of the cost changes from CY 2016 to the Historic Test 
6 
Year, Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 illustrates that increased costs for the 
7 
electric and gas businesses over the 2016 through Historic Test Year period are 
8 
attributable to costs directly incurred at the Company of$215 million for electric 
9 
and $85 million for gas.  Costs incurred from the Service Company and other 
10 
companies decreased for electric by $8 million and $12 million, respectively 
11 
and increased for gas by $10 million and $2 million, respectively.

10 
Q. 
Please explain the methodology for developing the forecast of O&M 
11 
expenses in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
12 
A. 
To develop the O&M forecasts, the Company began by determining the costs 
13 
incurred in the Historic Test Year for the various expense types.  Next, the 
14 
Company reviewed Historic Test Year charges to determine whether specific 
15 
costs should be normalized, for example, as out-of-period or one-time charges.  
16 
The inflation factors set forth in Exhibit __ (RRP-8) were then applied to the 
17 
majority of expense types to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years.  Forecasts 
18 
of certain expenses were developed using a more comprehensive methodology 
19 
than adjusting for inflation.  For example, labor expense was developed by 
20 
annualizing the monthly and weekly employees on payroll as of the end of the 
21 


--- Page 40 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 37 of 146 
Historic Test Year, adjusting for known changes to the employee headcount, 
1 
and applying contractual and projected wage increases to forecast the Rate Year 
2 
and Data Years.  Additionally, the Company adjusted forecast O&M expenses 
3 
to reflect incremental work projected for the Rate Year or costs associated with 
4 
new initiatives.   
5 
 
6 
Q. 
What assumptions did the Company make regarding non-labor inflation? 
7 
A. 
Except where specifically identified otherwise, the Company applied the non-
8 
labor inflation factor of 2.880 percent to all non-labor expenses in the Historic 
9 
Test Year to forecast the Rate Year.  This factor is equivalent to a 1.152 percent 
10 
average annual increase between the Historic Test Year and the Rate Year.  The 
11 
Company applied the non-labor inflation factor of 2.109 percent to forecast 
12 
Data Year 1 and 2.280 percent to forecast Data Year 2.  These factors represent 
13 
the forecast change in the GDP Chained Price Index obtained from Moody’s, 
14 
as provided in Exhibit ___ (RRP-8).  The Panel addresses calculation of the 
15 
non-labor inflation factor later in its testimony.

A.

12

13

14 
National Grid affiliates (including Niagara Mohawk) that receive the services.  
15 
For example, when the Service Company performs a service for the benefit of 
16 
a single company, that company is directly charged for that service.  If the 
17 
service is for the benefit of multiple companies, however, the charge is allocated 
18

19

20 
Service Company.

Q. 
Please describe how the Service Company charged Niagara Mohawk for 
8 
services during the Historic Test Year. 
9 
A. 
Service Company charges were either directly charged to Niagara Mohawk or, 
10 
when a service was performed for multiple affiliates, charges were aggregated 
11 
and allocated to all affiliates that benefited from the service using approved 
12 
allocation methodologies.  These allocations have been developed to 
13 
accommodate the different types of costs that are charged by the Service 
14 
Company.  
15 
 
16 
 
The allocators are based on cost causation principles and are designed to 
17 
maximize use of direct allocation codes where charges have been incurred for 
18 
the direct benefit of a single company.  When it is not appropriate to use a direct 
19 
allocation code, a cost causative code is assigned based on the appropriate 
20 
causation driver.  Where it is not appropriate to use a direct or cost causative 
21 


--- Page 45 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 42 of 146 
code, then a general allocator is used.  The general allocator used by the Service 
1 
Company is based on a three-point model using Net Margin, Net Plant, and Net 
2 
O&M expense.  These allocation principles are set forth in the National Grid’s 
3 
Cost Allocation Manual.

GBE Program 
1 
Q. 
What is the GBE Program? 
2 
A. 
The GBE Program is a program to develop and implement a comprehensive 
3 
framework of new information technology and business process changes 
4 
necessary to strengthen and improve the performance of National Grid’s U.S. 
5 
gas business.  The GBE Program is supported by the Gas Infrastructure and 
6 
Operations Panel. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Is the Company proposing to update the GBE Program Total Cost Cap 
9 
that was established in the 2017 Rate Case? 
10 
A. 
Yes, the Company is proposing to increase the GBE Program spending cap from 
11 
$458.1 million to $530.9 million. 
12 
 
13 
Q. 
Please explain the reason for this update. 
14 
A. 
The GBE Program will develop Service Company owned assets that will be 
15 
used by and benefit multiple operating companies. The spending cap 
16 
established in the 2017 Rate Case represented the approximate level of Service 
17 
Company costs that would yield an appropriate level of revenue requirement 
18 
attributable and chargeable to Niagara Mohawk for its relative share of the GBE 
19 
Program.  The GBE Program revenue requirement allocated to Niagara 
20 


--- Page 55 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 52 of 146 
Mohawk was based on applying the allocation rates in effect at the time the 
1 
2017 Rate Case was filed to the $458.1 million cap.    
2 
 
3 
While GBE Program costs have increased, the proportional allocation of those 
4 
costs to Niagara Mohawk has decreased.  Applying the lower allocation 
5 
percentage to the Program Total Cost Cap would result in a lower allocation of 
6 
costs to Niagara Mohawk than was established in the 2017 Rate Case.  
7 
Therefore, the Company is proposing to update the Program Total Cost Cap 
8 
such that Niagara Mohawk’s updated allocation results in the allocation of costs 
9 
at the same level approved by the Commission in the 2017 Rate Case.  In this 
10 
way, customers will pay no more and no less than the costs approved by the 
11 
Commission for recovery.   
12 
 
13 
Q. 
How did the Company determine the updated Program Total Cost Cap? 
14 
A. 
The Company used the forecast/allocations for both operating expense and 
15 
capital expense from the 2017 Rate Case and updated those allocations with 
16 
current allocation percentage.  The Company found that the revenue 
17 
requirement impact was significantly lower with the updated allocation 
18 
percentages compared to what was agreed upon in the 2017 Rate Case.  The 
19 
Company’s analysis found an under recovery of 13.99 percent from an 
20 
operating expense revenue requirement perspective and 18.76 percent from a 
21 


--- Page 56 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 53 of 146 
capital expense (Service Company Rents) perspective from the 2017 Rate Case 
1 
allocations. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
How did the Company apply the findings from this analysis to calculate the 
4 
updated Program Total Cost Cap for both operating expense and capital 
5 
expense?  
6 
A. 
The Company applied the 13.99 percent (calculated under recovery for 
7 
operating expense) to the GBE operating expense portion of the Program Total 
8 
Cost Cap.  This would have changed the operating expense portion from $128.9 
9 
million to a proposed $147 million, but, because the current GBE Program 
10 
estimates the total operating expense to be $140 million, the Company aligned 
11 
the operating expense portion of the Program Total Cost Cap to be at the final 
12 
forecast amount (a $6.8 million reduction). The Company then applied the 
13 
18.76 percent (calculated under recovery for capital expense) to the GBE 
14 
Program capital expense portion of the Program Total Cost Cap.  This would 
15

Please describe 53rd week labor costs. 
10 
A. 
Every five years there is an additional, or 53rd, pay week.  Therefore, an amount 
11 
equal to one-fifth of the weekly cost (i.e., one day) is added to the labor cost to 
12 
reflect the normalized cost of the 53rd week.  Fifty-third week labor costs are 
13 
associated with any employee who is paid weekly.  Typically, these are 
14 
represented employees.  The 53rd week labor costs are added to the total Rate 
15 
Year represented labor costs found on Pages 8 and 9 of Schedule 23.   
16 
 
17 
Q. 
How were 53rd week labor costs calculated? 
18 
A. 
53rd week labor costs were calculated by taking the estimated annual Rate Year 
19 
labor costs for weekly paid employees divided by 2,080 hours and multiplied 
20 
by eight hours.  The 2,080 hours represents the total number of hours worked 
21 


--- Page 76 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 73 of 146 
in a normal CY and the eight hours represents the normal work hours in a day 
1 
(i.e., one-fifth of the week).  The calculation was performed by salary band for 
2 
full time represented employees and part time represented employees.

21 


--- Page 77 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 74 of 146 
A. 
Transportation lease expense consists of vehicles on lease in the Historic Test 
1

Q. 
How did the Company develop the forecast for transportation lease 
8 
expense? 
9 
A. 
The Company began with the vehicle inventory as of December 31, 2019.  From 
10

11

12

13

14

15

16

18 
Q.

19 
A.

20 
additional vehicles along with projected acquisition costs.  Lease expenses are 
21 


--- Page 78 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 75 of 146 
then calculated using the acquisition cost, term of the lease, and projected 
1

2 
 
3 
Q. 
Why did the Company not simply adjust the Historic Test Year for 
4 
inflation to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years? 
5 
A. 
The Company does not believe that adjusting for inflation provides an accurate 
6 
projection of activity in the Rate Year and Data Years.  Transportation lease 
7 
expense is impacted by changes in the Company’s fleet.  Specifically, increases 
8 
or decreases in lease expense result from vehicles being removed, replaced, or 
9 
added to the Company’s fleet.  In addition, the Company’s fleet is comprised 
10 
of many different types of vehicles and equipment.  These vehicles vary in costs 
11 
and lease terms.  The Company’s forecast takes into account these known and 
12 
measurable changes and, therefore, provides a more accurate and reasonable 
13 
forecast than simply adjusting for inflation.  
14

V. 
Efficiency and Productivity Cost Reductions 
16 
Q. 
Please describe National Grid’s efforts to reduce costs. 
17 
A. 
National Grid is committed to continuously identifying opportunities to be 
18 
more efficient and productive for the benefit of its customers.  To that end, in 
19 
advance of these rate filings, National Grid undertook an aggressive cost 
20 
efficiency program, known as the Accelerate Program, to reduce customers’ 
21 


--- Page 90 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 87 of 146 
energy bills.  This proactive effort proved invaluable in light of the economic 
1 
impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in savings to customers in these 
2 
rate filings of approximately $35 million in the Rate Year and each of the Data 
3 
Years, or approximately $105 million in efficiencies over the term of the 
4 
proposed rate plan (excluding inflation).  This level of savings resulting from 
5 
the Accelerate Program is unprecedented and far in excess of those typically 
6 
included in a one-year case.  While the pandemic will undoubtedly challenge 
7 
the Company’s ability to deliver these savings, as the current focus has been 
8 
on work necessary to maintain safe and reliable service, the Company is 
9 
nevertheless reflecting the full forecast of aspirational savings as a means to 
10 
mitigate rate impacts during this challenging time.  These savings are also 
11 
incremental to the productivity adjustment of approximately $37 million over 
12 
the term of the proposed rate plan, which is discussed below.     
13 
    
14 
Q. 
Please describe the Accelerate Program. 
15 
A. 
In FY 2019, National Grid announced an ambitious, three-year efficiency 
16 
challenge called the Accelerate Program, which set out an aspirational target 
17 
of a 20 percent efficiency improvement in O&M and capital expenses across 
18 
the U.S. business by FY 2021.  The Accelerate Program is aimed at improving 
19 
both the quality and cost-effectiveness of National Grid’s services to 
20 
customers.  This ambitious target was purposefully set to drive maximum 
21 


--- Page 91 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 88 of 146 
customer value and at the end of FY 2020 National Grid has managed to 
1 
achieve around half of this aspirational target.   
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Why did the Company undertake this initiative? 
4 
 A. 
Affordability is a significant concern for customers.  At the same time, we 
5 
need to make investments to modernize the system and implement new 
6 
programs and technologies to meet the changing energy landscape.  These 
7 
include investments to replace outdated systems, modernize the electric and 
8 
gas networks, implement new digital solutions, and enable renewable energy 
9 
sources to meet the goals of the CLCPA.  The need for these investments must 
10 
be balanced against the financial impacts on customers.  To address these 
11 
competing concerns, National Grid launched the Accelerate Program.  The 
12 
Accelerate Program is National Grid’s effort to identify efficiencies to enable 
13 
ongoing critical investments and support the State’s long-term policy and 
14 
sustainability objectives, while mitigating customers’ energy costs in a manner 
15 
that maintains affordability.  
16 
 
17 
Q. 
How is National Grid attempting to achieve its efficiency target? 
18 
A. 
National Grid undertook a variety of initiatives across its U.S. operations to 
19 
standardize processes and reduce costs.  Example initiatives undertaken 
20 
include programs that: 
21 


--- Page 92 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 89 of 146 
• Reduced property tax expense; 
1 
• Delivered capital projects more efficiently; 
2 
• Optimized office space;  
3 
• Reduced contractor and consultant costs; 
4 
• Reduced material and fleet costs; and 
5 
• Utilized tools and technology to drive efficiencies. 
6 
 
7 
All of the Accelerate Program initiatives are being tracked in a web-based tool, 
8 
known as Wave.  Wave contains various implementation levels, through 
9 
which initiatives must progress before a determination is made that the 
10 
initiative can be counted toward the targets.  A centralized repository for 
11 
identifying and tracking the progress of various Accelerate Program initiatives 
12 
provides transparency on the progress against targets and avoids overlap. 
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please explain the implementation levels used to track progress in the 
15 
Wave tool. 
16 
A. 
Each Accelerate Program initiative is placed at an implementation level (“IL”) 
17 
based on its stage of development, from purely an idea (IL 0) to fully 
18 
implemented (IL 5).  ILs 0 through 2 cover the stages of idea formulation to 
19 
an initial estimate of potential benefits.  In these stages, teams brainstorm 
20 
initiatives to be evaluated as opportunities to deliver process improvements, 
21 


--- Page 93 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 90 of 146 
assigning a rough estimate of the potential benefit as an initial proxy until 
1 
better information is developed to quantify the benefit.  Teams are encouraged 
2 
to include as many ideas as possible.  Therefore, many initiatives do not move 
3 
beyond IL 2.   The potential benefit becomes more refined when an initiative 
4 
advances to IL 3, where Finance validates that the initiative has the potential 
5 
to deliver savings, and the business puts together a plan to implement the 
6 
initiative.  An IL 3 benefit is still aspirational, however, as the initiative may 
7 
not be implemented for a variety of reasons.  For example, an initiative could 
8 
require a new contract to be negotiated with a vendor or the implementation 
9 
of a new IT solution; without the new contract or IT solution, the feasibility or 
10 
economics of the initiative may be impacted.  Similarly, in the process of 
11 
implementing the initiative, the business could realize that assumptions have 
12 
changed and therefore the initiative cannot be implemented. 
13 
 
14 
It is not until IL 4 where an initiative moves from conceptual to deliverable.  
15 
In IL 4, the business has completed all activities required to deliver the 
16 
initiative.  In IL 5, Finance has confirmed that savings have been realized and 
17 
the actual amount of the savings, which could have changed from the original 
18 
estimate.   
19 
 
 
20 


--- Page 94 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 91 of 146

Please explain how O&M savings from initiatives are reflected in the case. 
1 
A. 
The Company’s revenue requirements reflects O&M savings associated with 
2 
initiatives it believes are reasonably achievable and likely to deliver benefits 
3 
to customers, namely those in ILs 4 and 5.  Given the conceptual nature of the 
4 
initiatives in ILs 0 through 3, they are not reflected because it is unknown 
5 
whether they will be implemented, and, if they are, the extent to which any 
6 
savings will materialize.  
7 
 
8 
 
Exhibit ___ (RRP-11), Workpapers to Exhibit ___ (RRP-3), Schedule 33, 
9 
Workpaper 1 lists the initiatives, the affected operating companies, the 
10 
allocation of savings to Niagara Mohawk’s electric and gas businesses, 
11 
whether they were implemented in the Historic Test Year or will be in the 
12 
post-Historic Test Year period, and where in the revenue requirements the 
13

15 
Q. 
Has National Grid reflected Niagara Mohawk’s full share of O&M 
16 
savings from the Accelerate Program?

Q. 
Please explain the “Federal Income Tax Rate Change and Flowthrough” 
12 
tax only item the Company included in FIT expense. 
13 
A. 
On December 22, 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (the “Act”) was enacted 
14 
resulting in significant changes in federal income taxation for the Company.  
15 
Most notably, the federal income tax rate was reduced from 35 percent to 21 
16 
percent.  The Commission issued an “Order Instituting Proceeding” on 
17 
December 29, 2017, to address the impact on utility rates of the Act and to 
18 
express the intent of the Commission to preserve the net benefits of the Act for 
19 
customers.  In December 2017, the Company recorded the rate change reduction 
20 
to accumulated deferred income tax (“ADIT”) with an offset to an income tax 
21 


--- Page 107 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 104 of 146 
regulatory liability, recognizing that customers should receive the benefit of the 
1 
lower rate on the accumulated book-tax temporary differences.  After the filing 
2 
of the March 31, 2018 federal income tax return, the Company finalized the 
3 
ADIT rate change based on the final pre-rate change tax return data.  
4 
Subsequent minor adjustments have been made to the rate change liability as a 
5 
result of finalizing and accounting for the completion of the federal income tax 
6 
audit of FYs 2010 – 2012.  The Rate Year and Data Years include the 
7 
amortization of excess federal ADIT for the benefit of customers combined with 
8 
the flow through effect of other historical plant related timing differences such 
9 
as depreciation and cost of removal.  This amortization reduces the Company’s 
10 
effective tax rate and mitigates the rate increase to customers. 
11

Q.

13 
differences included with the amortization of federal excess ADIT? 
14 
A.

15 
cost of removal and equity AFUDC as flow through, affecting the net income 
16 
tax expense charged to customers.  To maintain the complexity of new timing 
17 
differences, the amortization into rates of the reversals of those timing 
18 
differences, and prior historic federal income tax rate changes, the Company 
19 
uses the deferred tax module within its PowerTax depreciation system.  Each 
20 
year, new timing differences are input into the system and the book depreciation 
21

1 
deferred tax to be normalized and the amount to be flowed through to

3 
implementation of the new federal income tax rate, the system is now showing 
4

5

6

B. 
Deferred Taxes 
16 
Q.

17

18

19 
 
 
20 


--- Page 117 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 114 of 146 
Q. 
How did the Company develop the forecast of ADIT? 
1 
A. 
The Company began with the actual electric and gas ADIT balances as of March 
2 
31, 2020, and calculated the forecast based on changes in plant and regulatory 
3 
assets and liabilities.  The Company then made additional adjustments for tax 
4 
amortizations to arrive at the forecast ADIT balances for the Rate Year and Data 
5 
Years, as shown on Exhibit __ (RRP-7), Schedule 3.   
6 
 
7 
Q. 
Please explain the change in ADIT related to plant movements. 
8 
A. 
The Company used its tax depreciation system, PowerTax, to forecast the tax 
9 
depreciation on historic plant balances as of March 31, 2019, the fiscal year end 
10 
of the most recently filed federal income tax return.  All additional changes in 
11 
ADIT related to plant are a direct result of forecast plant additions, forecast cost 
12 
of removal, and forecast book depreciation.  The Company forecast tax 
13 
deductions related to plant additions by calculating first, tax basis adjustments 
14 
and then, tax depreciation.  The basis adjustments are the new plant additions 
15 
eligible for the repair deduction and an estimate of contributions in aid of 
16 
construction (“CIAC”) income.  The repair rate was applied as a percentage of 
17 
total capital expenditures.  The percentage was an estimate based on a trend 
18 
analysis of the actual results of the prior three fiscal years’ tax return study for 
19 
capital plant repairs.  The CIAC tax basis adjustment was a percentage of total 
20 
capital expenditures and was an estimate based on the actual CIAC income 
21 


--- Page 118 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 115 of 146 
percentages from the prior three FYs’ tax returns.   The plant tax basis after 
1 
deductions for repairs and increases for CIAC was then subject to Modified 
2 
Accelerated Cost Recovery System (“MACRS”) depreciation, using a 20-year 
3 
tax life.  The Company also deducts cost of removal in the year the cash is spent.  
4 
All tax plant deductions were compared to book depreciation and federal and 
5 
state ADIT was computed on the temporary difference.  
6 
 
 
7 
Q. 
Why is bonus depreciation not included in the ADIT forecast? 
8 
A. 
Under the Act, regulated public utilities are generally prohibited from taking 
9 
bonus depreciation deductions on assets placed in service after September 27, 
10 
2017.  This provision was tied to the provision that permitted regulated public 
11 
utilities to be exempt from the interest expense limitations under new section 
12 
163(j).  The Company has interpreted the change in bonus depreciation statute 
13 
to allow bonus depreciation on self-constructed assets started prior to 
14 
September 28, 2017, under the prior bonus depreciation regulations using the 
15 
phased-out percentages of 50 percent through December 2017, 40 percent 
16 
through December 2018, and 30 percent through December 2019.  Included in 
17 
the ADIT balances for the Historic Test Year are the deferred tax effects of all 
18 
bonus depreciation deductions taken on plant under these regulations.  As the 
19 
Rate Year and Data Years occur after the expiration of the prior bonus 
20 


--- Page 119 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 116 of 146 
depreciation regulations, there are no bonus depreciation deductions used in the 
1 
computation of plant-related ADIT in the Rate Year or the Data Years.  
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Please explain the other discrete adjustments to rate base ADIT. 
4 
A. 
The Company is increasing rate base as the New York State income tax rate 
5 
change and State Year 2000 rate change are amortized through the income tax 
6 
expense component of the revenue requirement, as described above.  The 
7 
Company has also included the increase to rate base due to the amortization of 
8 
historical investment tax credit (“ITC”). 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
What other impact does tax reform have on rate base ADIT? 
11 
A. 
To maintain rate base neutrality after an income tax rate change, the Company 
12 
needs to include the tax regulatory liability in rate base along with the ADIT 
13 
that has been restated to the new 21 percent federal rate.  The Company has 
14 
included the entire rate change tax regulatory liability in rate base rather than 
15 
only the rate change related to underlying rate base items.  This methodology 
16 
will make it easier to track and audit the reversal of excess ADIT and make 
17 
calculations of carrying charges that are net of tax easier.  The Company will 
18 
leave the entire excess ADIT in the regulatory liability account until the 
19 
amortization begins in the Rate Year.  The average ADIT balances in the Rate 
20 


--- Page 120 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 117 of 146 
Year and Data Years include the reversals of excess ADIT that are included in 
1 
the income tax expense component of the revenue requirement. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
How did the Company reflect changes in regulatory assets and liabilities in 
4 
the forecast? 
5 
A. 
Because the change in most regulatory assets and liabilities results in a book-
6 
tax timing difference, the existing deferred tax balances on the regulatory 
7 
accounts included in rate base were adjusted by any forecast change in those 
8 
accounts in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
9

C. 
Working Capital 
11 
Q. 
Has the Company recognized a working capital allowance associated with 
12 
electric power and gas purchases? 
13 
A. 
Yes.  Schedule 5 of Exhibit __ (RRP-7) presents the calculation of the carrying 
14 
charge applicable to the working capital requirements associated with electric 
15 
power and gas purchases based on the lead-lag studies contained in this 
16 
schedule.  The Company used the same methodology as was approved by the 
17 
Commission in the 2017 Rate Case for the electric and gas studies.    
18 
 
 
19 


--- Page 121 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 118 of 146 
Q. 
What are the lead-lag studies used to measure? 
1 
A. 
The lead-lag studies are used to measure the working capital needed by the 
2 
Company to support its electric power and gas purchases.  The Company is 
3 
required to provide working capital for the time between when the Company 
4 
pays its suppliers for electric power and gas purchases and the time the 
5 
Company receives payments for these purchases from its customers.  The 
6 
results of the studies are used to determine the working capital necessary for 
7 
purchased electric power and gas expense.   
8

XI. 
Inflation Factors 
8 
Q. 
Please explain Exhibit __ (RRP-8). 
9 
A. 
Exhibit __ (RRP-8) sets forth the table of inflation factors used to escalate 
10 
expense and capital expenditures for the electric and gas businesses from the 
11 


--- Page 137 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 134 of 146 
Historic Test Year to the Rate Year and Data Years.  The exhibit consists of a 
1 
Summary Page detailing the escalation rates.  
2 
 
3 
Q. 
What inflation adjustment did the Company use for O&M expense? 
4 
A. 
The inflation adjustment factor for determining the level of O&M expense in 
5 
the Rate Year is 2.8800 percent.  This is equivalent to 1.1520 percent average 
6 
annual increase between the Historic Test Year and the Rate Year. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
How was this inflation adjustment factor calculated? 
9 
A. 
The calculation is detailed in Exhibit __ (RRP-8).  The approach uses the GDP 
10 
Chained Price Index (“GDPIPD”) as the measure of the price level and percent 
11 
changes in this index as the measure of inflation.  The GDPIPD is released 
12 
quarterly by the US Department of Commerce, Department of Economic 
13 
Analysis.  The inflation adjustment factor is calculated by relating the average 
14 
of the GDPIPD in the Historic Test Year (the four quarters ended December 31, 
15 
2019) to forecast GDPIPD in the Rate Year (the four quarters ended June 30, 
16 
2022).  Inflation between the Historic Test Year and Data Years was calculated 
17 
in a similar fashion.

XII. 
Proposed Treatment of Existing Regulatory Deferral Accounts and New 
1 
Reconciliation Mechanisms 
2 
Q. 
Please describe the use and nature of regulatory deferral accounts. 
3 
A. 
Regulatory deferral accounts are used to track and reconcile expenses and 
4 
associated revenue recoveries to ensure that the appropriate amount of costs are 
5 
recovered from, or returned to, customers.  As discussed above and in Appendix 
6 
A, Niagara Mohawk has a number of deferral accounts previously created 
7 
pursuant to various Commission orders.  This section of the testimony will 
8 
discuss: 
9 
(i) 
the Company’s proposals to maintain or discontinue existing electric 
10 
and gas deferral accounts; 
11 
(ii) 
the Company’s proposals to revise certain existing electric and gas 
12 
deferral accounts; 
13 
(iii) 
the Company’s proposals to implement new regulatory reconciliation 
14 
mechanisms that address discrete issues; 
15 
(iv) 
the Company’s proposals to include a return on any balances in the 
16 
deferral accounts using the weighted average cost of capital for Niagara 
17 
Mohawk established in this proceeding; and 
18 
(v) 
the Company’s proposed recovery mechanism for these accounts.    
19 
 
20

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel

Q. 
Why did the Company incur interest expense as a result of the resolution 
1 
of a federal audit? 
2 
A. 
During the fiscal year ending March 31, 2009, National Grid NA adopted a new 
3 
method of tax accounting to deduct certain book capitalized expenditures as 
4 
routine repair and maintenance expenses.  The benefits of the change were 
5 
deferred and passed back to Niagara Mohawk’s customers.  In the FY 2010-
6 
2012 Tax Audit, it was determined that a portion of the repair tax deduction had 
7 
been taken in error.  As a result, the Company’s taxable income for the three 
8 
fiscal years with respect to the repair adjustment was increased by 
9 
$139,830,869, and the Company was required to pay additional taxes of 
10 
$48,941,154 as well as interest of $24,747,243, of which $19,797,794 is 
11 
attributable to the electric business and $4,949,449 is attributable to the gas 
12 
business.  As the Company’s customers received the benefits associated with 
13 
the repairs deduction, it is appropriate that the Company be permitted to defer 
14 
for future recovery the interest costs arising from the subsequent reversal of the 
15 
deduction that gave rise to these benefits. 
16 
 
17 
The Company proposes to modify the following existing deferral mechanisms: 
18 
• As discussed in the Shared Services Panel’s direct testimony, the 
19 
Company is proposing to continue the current property tax 
20 
reconciliation but modify it to a full symmetrical reconciliation 
21 


--- Page 143 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 140 of 146 
given the variability, uncertainty, and difficulties associated with 
1 
forecasting property tax expense. 
2 
 
3 
• The Company proposes two changes to the major storm deferral 
4 
mechanism:  (1) modify the current definition of a deferrable major 
5 
storm event to align with the definition of major storm used for 
6 
reliability reporting purposes; and (2) defer pre-staging costs 
7 
associated with storm events that do not meet the definition of a 
8 
deferrable major storm event.  Further details of these proposed 
9 
changes, including thresholds on pre-staging costs and number of

11 
Infrastructure and Operations Panel.

Q. 
Why are pension and OPEB assets and liabilities exempt from carrying 
8

9 
A.

10

11 
Because the Company does not advance cash to fund the deferred amount, no 
12 
carrying charge is warranted.  When the Company recovers the deferral, it 
13 
places the funds into the pension or OPEB trusts.

XIII. 
FERC Order 1000 Projects 
1 
Q. 
What ratemaking treatment has been applied to the Western New York 
2 
(“WNY”) Public Policy Transmission Needs (“PPTN”) Project? 
3 
A. 
The Company has modeled the capital, O&M, and offsetting revenue 
4 
components of its revenue requirement to match development of the project 
5 
C079236 to rebuild and reconductor the Niagara-Packard Lines 193/194 lines.  
6 
Specifically, Niagara Mohawk, as a Load Serving Entity in the New York 
7 
Independent System Operation (“NYISO”), will be allocated costs for the 
8 
WNYFC and paid by its retail load similar to the recovery of other NYISO 
9 
charges under Rule 46 of its tariff.  The Company proposes to retain the FERC 
10 
return on equity for this project because this will preserve the FERC ordered 
11 
cost allocation that represents a beneficiary pay principle where Company 
12 
would be allocated the same rate as other wholesale transmission service 
13 
customers paying for the WNY PPTN project and no more or less than what 
14

Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to retain the FERC return on equity for 
1 
these assets? 
2 
A. 
If the Commission were to use the retail rate process, it would impermissibly 
3 
prevent the Company from realizing the full FERC-approved ROE in the 
4 
NYISO Open Access Transmission Transfer (“RS17”) and use revenues paid 
5 
by jurisdictional loads/customers in other parts of the state to reduce the 
6 
payment to Niagara Mohawk retail customers.  Retaining the FERC ROE also 
7 
ensures a level playing field for incumbent and non-incumbent transmission 
8 
developers competing in the NYISO Order 1000. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
What is the proposed ratemaking treatment for the AC Proceeding 
11 
Projects? 
12 
A. 
The Company will directly recover the costs associated with the disposition of 
13 
the physical property assets directly from the project developers and credit 
14 
corresponding plant accounts.  With respect to real property, the Company will 
15 
either lease, grant an easement, or sell the affected real property to the developer 
16 
to allow for project development.  Depending on the real property transactions, 
17 
the Company will credit corresponding plant accounts and/or credit lease 
18 
revenue accounts. The Company will also recover the support, engineering, and 
19 
O&M costs required for the projects directly from the developers to ensure 
20 
Company customers are not subsidizing third-party development costs.  
21

Storm Restoration Costs 
Basis for the Deferral 
The Joint Proposal approved by the Commission in March 2018 in the Electric and Gas 
Rate Cases (“Joint Proposal”)2 covering the three-year period ending March 31,  2021, set an 
annual base rate allowance for major storm expense.  The Company reconciles the base rate 
allowance against the incremental major storm costs that are subject to recovery in accordance 
with Section 10.1.15 and Appendix 5, Schedule 10 of the Joint Proposal.  To determine if costs 
can be charged to the deferral account, the storm event must qualify as a “major storm” and the 
costs must be incremental.  Any over or under recoveries are deferred for refund to, or recovery 
from, customers.

Auction Debt True Up - Electric 
Basis for the Deferral 
Niagara Mohawk’s capital structure includes variable rate pollution control revenue 
bonds.  The interest rate for these bonds is periodically reset using an auction process that 
provides for a default rate if the auctions fail.  The Joint Proposal established an annual rate 
allowance for these interest costs for rate year one only, and the Company continued to reconcile 
the actual interest expense with the amount reflected in rates in accordance with Section 10.1.5 
of the Joint Proposal.  Any over or under recoveries are deferred for refund to, or recovery from, 
customers.  This deferral will be discontinued after rate year one of the Joint Proposal and 
replaced by the Long-Term Debt True Up Deferral for rate years two and three.

Basis for the Deferral

Auction Debt True-Up – Gas 
Basis for the Deferral 
Niagara Mohawk’s capital structure includes variable rate pollution control revenue 
bonds.  The interest rate for these bonds is periodically reset using an auction process that 
provides for a default rate if the auctions fail.  The Joint Proposal established an annual rate 
allowance for these interest costs for rate year one only, and the Company continued to reconcile 
the actual interest expense with the amount reflected in rates in accordance with Section 10.1.5 
of the Joint Proposal.  Any over or under recoveries are deferred for refund to, or recovery from, 
customers.  This deferral will be discontinued after rate year one of the Joint Proposal and 
replaced by the Long-Term Debt True Up Deferral for rate years two and three.

customers after the change to the amount of state income tax recorded by each utility until base 
rates were reset.  The difference was deferred with carrying charges. The transition mechanism 
continued until September 1, 2003, when the tax change was reflected in gas rates for Niagara

Oswego Purchase Power Agreement (“PPA”) 
Basis for the Deferral 
In 1993, the Company entered into a thirty (30) year PPA with the City of Oswego to 
purchase power at fixed rate.  Under a tracking provision in the PPA, the City is required to pay 
the Company the difference between the fixed contract rate and the cost the Company would 
have incurred if it had produced the power itself.  On a monthly basis, using a discounting 
schedule, the regulatory liability will wind down until the PPA’s expiration in December 2023 
based on the difference between the fixed contract rate and the internal production rate for 
monthly production and the amount withheld/prepaid monthly by the City of Oswego.

Commodity Timing Adjustment 
The Company reconciles its electric commodity costs through the Electricity Supply 
Reconciliation Mechanism (“ESRM”) pursuant to PSC 220 Rule 46.3.  This mechanism 
calculates the deferral by comparing the prior month actual electric supply costs and the prior 
month sales revenue. The Commodity Timing Adjustment eliminates the one month lag between 
recovery through the ESRM and the revenue and power costs recorded in the general ledger.

Nuclear Fuel Disposal Costs 
Basis for the Deferral 
 
As addressed in Case 98-E-0405, the federal government requires utility companies that 
operate nuclear plants to pay a 0.1 cent/kWh fee to cover the cost of removing and permanently 
disposing of spent nuclear fuel.  This charge is avoided when a plant is permanently shut down 
and ceases to produce energy.  Thus, the spent nuclear fuel disposal fee is a “to go” cost.  It is 
recognized, however, that the federal government keeps track of the amounts contributed by each 
utility toward the disposal of spent nuclear fuel for each nuclear plant.   
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2019 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2019, was a credit of $176.921 million. 
Forecast of Deferrals through June 30, 2021 
 
As of June 30, 2021, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $177.943 million.  This is 
the result of additional interest being accrued to the liability.

As of June 30, 2021, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $3.635 million. 
 
Gas Safety Performance Metric (“GSPM”) Penalties 
Basis for the Deferral 
 
Sections 10.1.8 and 12 of the Joint Proposal establish Gas Safety Performance Metrics  
 
negative or positive revenue adjustments.  Niagara Mohawk’s gas safety performance will be 
measured for each calendar year against a set of Gas Safety Performance Metrics.  A total of 150 
pre-tax basis points will be at risk per calendar year for performance under metrics laid out in 
Section 12.  Any Gas Safety Performance Metrics negative revenue adjustments incurred by 
Niagara Mohawk will be deferred for future use in incremental gas safety programs, as discussed 
in Section 10.1.8.  
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2019 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2019, was a credit of $2.684 million. 
Forecast of Deferral through June 30, 2021 
The Company has not forecast any additional changes to the account balance. 
 
Paige Street Deferral  
Basis for the Deferral 
Pursuant to rate case 15-G-0171, the Company and the Commission negotiated a Joint Proposal 
which, among other things, established a regulatory liability of $0.500 million borne by the 
shareholders to fund a Remote Meter Valve Pilot project for the benefit of the customers. This 
settlement and Joint Proposal related to a natural gas incident at 310 Paige Street, Schenectady.

Gas Rate Plan Deferral Credit  
Basis for the Deferral

deferral balance in the amount of $56.1 million. The credits will allow for a gradual transition  
 
to full cost-of-service rates as reflected in Appendix 3, Schedules 2 and 3. This amount will be  
 
amortized over fiscal years 2019 through 2022.

Unbilled Revenue – Gas 
Basis for the Deferral 
Unbilled revenue represents the unbilled portion of the current month’s revenues.  This is 
a result of cycle billing and the fact that customers are not billed for current month usage but for 
their last 30 days of use.  Customers are billed over 20 cycles during each calendar month. 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2019 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2019, was a debit of $21.431 million. 
Forecast of Deferrals through June 30, 2021 
The Company has not forecast any additional changes to the account balance.

Basis for the Deferral

capitalized and amortized.

Executive summary 
In preparation for NMPC rate case filing, a detailed and thorough review of the test year transactions (“Financial 
Review”) was performed.  
This document outlines the testing approach and results of the Financial Review of test year transactions incurred 
by the Companies, led by internal resources within the National Grid Finance Team (the “Finance Team”).  
Scope of our examination 
Our examination is designed to cover subject matter that includes transactions recorded by the following 
subsidiaries of the National Grid USA:  
 
NMPC 
 
Service Company 
For each entity, the Financial Review report comprises of a Summary of Selected Vendor Costs, a Summary of 
Selected Labor Costs, Employee Expense Costs, and Manual Journal Entries for the twelve-month period ended 
December 31, 2019. 
Risk and approach  
The Finance Team performed a sampling and testing approach consistent with the manner performed for prior 
cases filed with the Commission to address the risks identified in each area of testing.   
Our testing approach was designed to mirror that of an independent external audit. Though the Financial Review 
is being performed by National Grid employees, and is therefore not fully independent, the test is not being 
performed by those who have operated the related controls, nor recorded the related transactions and therefore 
does have a substantial degree of independence from business process owners.   
Results and findings  
Our results and findings are detailed in the Results and Findings section. The findings include net amounts of 
$0.4 million related to NMPC (See section “Results and Findings- NMPC”) and $0.06 million related to Service 
Company (See section “Results and Findings- Service Company”).    
Exhibit______(RRP-2)
Schedule 2
Page 3 of 88


--- Page 233 ---
 
 
 
Risk and approach 
The subject matter included in the Summary of Costs reports was developed as follows: 
Vendor costs – The population for testing for vendor costs was from a list of amounts approved for payment 
to each vendor in each of the four quarters of calendar year 2019.  Items were selected for testing using a 
risk-based sampling approach, to cover a large number of unique transactions and high number of vendors. 
A unique transaction was defined as a vendor’s work for a particular project with a particular department 
at National Grid (e.g. If a vendor was performing work for one department under ten different projects, they 
would each be considered a unique transaction of which we would obtain 40 percent coverage [i.e. 4 
projects].  A minimum of 10 (NMPC) and 15 (Service Company) percent of the number of invoices 
associated with each of the unique transactions selected for testing would also be examined).  Vendors 
which aggregated to less than $100 thousand dollars (0.2% and 0.4% of the total population for NMPC and 
Service Company, respectively) were considered de minimis and therefore, not sampled. 
Labor costs (NMPC) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial report which 
included base time and overtime pay but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social security taxes, 
life insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and other welfare 
expenses. All base time and overtime pay were selected for inclusion in the subject matter considered for 
testing.     
Labor costs (Service Company) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial 
report which included base time and overtime pay but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social 
security taxes, life insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and 
other welfare expenses. Given the large volume of transactions, items were selected that represented (i) the 
15 largest cost centers based on payroll costs incurred and (ii) 25 cost centers selected without bias ranked 
greater than 15. 
Employee expense costs – The population for testing for employee expense costs was based on a financial 
report of amounts approved for payment in each quarter. Items were selected that represent the top 25 single 
employee claims (“trip reports”) and top 50 purchase credit card (“P-card”) transactions based on dollars 
approved for payment in each quarter, 15 trip reports selected without bias ranked between 26 and 100 
based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, 10 trip reports selected without bias ranked greater 
than 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, and 25 P-card transactions selected without 
bias ranked greater than 50 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter. The Summary of 
Selected Employee Expense Costs did not include any expenses submitted for reimbursement by “Band A” 
employees, defined as senior executives of NGUSA, as well as other costs which were excluded following 
a keyword search – as these costs are not sought for recovery by the Company.  
General ledger entries – Testing for manual journal entries was based on a financial report of all journal 
entries that impacted manual journal accounts. For each system “document type” included in the list, items 
were identified for selection and presentation in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries based on 
dollar value, as detailed in the Notes to each of the Summary of Costs reports.

Cost area Test objective 
Test details 
Vendor 
costs 
To test the financial records that 
vendor costs are incurred and 
accurate 
1. Compare costs recorded in the ledger to underlying 
vendor support (invoice or similar). 
To test the financial records that 
vendor costs are allocated to the 
correct company 
2. Review the underlying vendor information for details 
of goods purchased or services performed and 
identify whether the goods or services relate to / 
benefit the entity to which they were charged. 
To test the financial records that 
costs related to capital programs or 
operating 
expenses 
are 
appropriately classified 
3. Review the underlying vendor information for details 
of whether goods purchased, or services performed 
related to a capital program or not. 
Labor 
costs 
To test the financial records that 
labor costs are accurate 
4.  Testing employee hourly pay rates with reference to 
employee compensation arrangement information. 
5. Review monthly payroll totals and identify any outlier 
information, obtain explanation for any unusual 
fluctuations and test that they are reasonable. 
To test the financial records that 
payroll costs are charged to Service 
Company orders consistent with 
work performed (Service Company 
only) 
6. Review amounts charged by employees charging 
Service Company “X” orders and test whether the 
allocation charged is consistent with the employee’s 
job title and functional area. 
7. Perform analytics by employees and compare with the 
average pay rate for each grade to identify and 
investigate any unusual fluctuations 
To test the financial records that 
labor costs are allocated to the 
correct companies (NMPC 
only) 
8. Perform analytics by employees and compare with the 
average pay rate for each grade to identify and 
investigate any unusual fluctuations. 
9. Review time capture records for all employees over 
the 12-month period; metrics obtained were applied 
to identify outlier entries (e.g. more than 12 hours in 
a day, hours worked between midnight and 4 am, 
multiple 
entities 
charged 
in 
a 
day, 
order/region/segment/ company charged which is 
inconsistent with the employee’s job title and 
functional area). Inquiry procedures were performed 
to investigate inconsistencies. 
Employee 
expenses 
To test the financial records that 
employee expenses are accurate 
and submitted consistent with the 
Company policy 
10.Obtain the claim information and supporting 
documents submitted; compare such documents to 
the requirements of the Company policy.  
11.Verify the expenses are allocated to a reasonable 
order based on the employee’s job title and functional 
area.  
 
Journal 
entries 
To test the financial records that 
the journal entries presented are 
accurately calculated and reflect 
the underlying transaction 
12. Obtain copies of the approved journal entry 
submission and test that the entry ties to the 
underlying support. Review and recalculate elements 
of the underlying support to test its accuracy.

Notes to the Summary of Costs 
1.Background 
 
a. NMPC 
 
 
Niagara Mohawk Power Corporation d/b/a National Grid NY (“NMPC”) provides gas and electric services to 
customers in upstate New York. 
 
The Company is a wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid USA (“NGUSA”). NGUSA is a public utility 
holding company with regulated subsidiaries engaged in the generation of electricity and the transmission, 
distribution, and sale of both natural gas and electricity. NGUSA is a direct wholly-owned subsidiary of 
National Grid North America Inc. (NGNA) and an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid plc, a 
public limited company incorporated under the laws of England and Wales. 
 
The Company separately issues financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting requirements 
of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) as set forth in its applicable Uniform System of 
Accounts and published accounting releases (together, the FERC USoA), as well as financial statements 
prepared in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (GAAP). The subject 
matter presented in the Summary of Costs is prepared consistently described in notes 2 to 5 below, which are 
not necessarily the same as the accounting requirements of the FERC USoA or GAAP. 
 
b. Service Company 
 
National Grid USA Service Company (“Service Company”) provides management, administrative, 
accounting, legal, engineering and other services to NG USA subsidiaries. 
 
National Grid USA Service Company (Servco), a wholly-owned subsidiary of NGUSA, provides management, 
administrative, accounting, legal, engineering, and other services to other NGUSA subsidiaries, including the 
Company. Servco provides its services on an “at cost” basis, determined using billing methods based on cost 
causative factors pursuant to service agreements and its Cost Allocation Manual, as further discussed in Note 
6. 
 
 
2. Vendor Costs 
 
Summary of Selected Vendor Costs – During each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2019 to 
December 31, 2019, NMPC approved payments to third party vendors totaling $2,670,088,030 and 
$1,927,157,254 for NMPC and Service Company, respectively. The Summary of Selected Vendor Costs 
represents vendor costs “approved for payment” during each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2019 
to December 31, 2019, related to the selected vendors listed. Irrespective of when the goods or services were 
received, for purposes of this presentation, vendor costs are considered approved for payment upon: 
 
 
internal acknowledgment that the goods or services have been received, and 
 
payment of the invoice. 
 
The subject matter excludes amounts approved for payment related to purchased commodity as these costs 
generally are not recovered via the Company’s base delivery rates. 
 
To capture and account for vendor costs, the Company initiates work orders under two types of projects, (1) 
capital projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs incurred in the execution of the 
Company’s capital programs, and (2) expense projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs 
incurred in the performance of non-capital-related activity. The subject matter and basis of accounting reflects 
the initial determination of whether the vendor costs were assigned to capital projects or expense projects. 
System-generated entries (generally related to the allocation of engineering-related work order design

All costs included in the Summary of Selected Vendor Costs have been “approved for payment” by the

considered “approved for payment” during the period presented, nor included in the accompanying Summary 
of Selected Vendor Costs. This accounting policy, applied in the Summary of Costs, is a basis of accounting 
other than GAAP and the FERC USoA. 
 
Upon satisfaction of the conditions approving a cost for payment, the cost is assigned to a work order as

 
Costs incurred in support of the Company’s capital program are assigned to work orders capturing costs 
under capital projects. 
 
 
Costs related solely to operating activities are assigned to work orders capturing costs under expense 
projects, or internal orders capturing expense items specific to the Company and incurred outside of the 
Company’s capital program. 
 
3. Labor Costs 
 
Summary of Selected Labor Costs – During the period from January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2019, recorded 
costs to employees of $467,722,263 and $530,438,537 for NMPC and Service Company, respectively, in 
consideration for work undertaken for the benefit of the Company. This amount includes base time and 
overtime pay but does not include labor-related overhead costs such as social security taxes, life insurance, 
pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and other welfare expenses. All base 
time and overtime pay was selected for inclusion in the subject matter to employees of the company or its 
affiliates for time charged during the period presented and have been allocated consistent with the Company’s 
Cost allocation Manual (Service Company only). Amounts presented in the Summary of Selected Labor Costs 
have been charged to capital and operating cost line items within the general ledger in a manner consistent 
with the nature of the work performed. 
 
Employees of the Company and its affiliates charge time to system work orders, similar to the process 
described above for vendor costs. Labor costs are recorded by the Company’s payroll and time capture system. 
Labor charges to work orders may be made by a direct employee of the Company, or by an employee of an 
affiliate company who is performing work for the benefit of the Company.

5. General Ledger Entries 
 
Summary of Selected Manual Journal Entries – During the period from January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2019, 
the Company recorded entries to the general ledger via automated journal entry and manual journal entry 
processes. Entries in the Company’s general ledgers are assigned a “document type” (doc type), a unique two-
digit code, designed to identify the source and nature of the journal entry. The complete population of operating 
expenses recorded is an aggregation of amounts recorded under all doc types to the relevant general ledger 
accounts. Costs approved for payment to vendors are recorded in the general ledger under doc types KR, RE, 
RS, and KG; labor costs are recorded under doc type AB; and employee expense costs under doc types TR 
and YU.  
 
Additional entries to the general ledger to allow the Company to maintain underlying books and records on a 
GAAP and FERC USoA basis are recorded via manual or automated entry under separate doc types.

“U6_“, “C40_”, “U40_”, “C411_” or“U411_”, excluding general ledger account C4000000 (Operating 
Revenue), and general ledger accounts related to income taxes. From this population, the method applied to

6. Costs incurred and allocated by Service Company 
 
Cost Allocation Manual and Service Agreements
